blocks.text: A **mutual fund** is an investment vehicle in which many investors **pool their money** to earn returns over a period. The pooled money (the **corpus**) is managed by an investment professional called the **fund manager** or **portfolio manager**, who invests it in bonds, stocks, gold and other assets. Gains (or losses) are **shared by the investors in proportion to their contribution**.

blocks.title: Key points
rows: A fund manager of an **Asset Management Company (AMC)**.
AMFI, the Association of Mutual Funds in India, is a self-regulatory body.
Securities such as shares, bonds, government securities, money market instruments, and gold.
The **Unit Trust of India (UTI)**, set up in **1963**.
Investors pay fees for professional management, much like paying a driver for chauffeuring.

blocks.title: Must-know
blocks.text: Mutual funds are **regulated by SEBI** (not the RBI or IRDAI). The fund is a **collective investment scheme** managed by an **AMC**. Returns are **not assured** and capital is **not protected**.

blocks.title: Not a depository
blocks.text: A mutual fund is **not** a depository financial intermediary like a bank. It does not accept deposits with a promised return, and it is regulated and sold to the general public as a market-linked scheme.

sections.title: Benefits of investing in mutual funds

blocks.title: Four main benefits
rows: A fund manager does the research on the economy, sectors and company financials, so investors who lack the skill or time can still invest.

Can earn **potentially higher returns** than traditional assured-return options, because returns are linked to the market. But a poor market hurts the investment and there is **no capital protection**.

Spreads risk instantly. Building a stock portfolio on your own needs at least **ten stocks** from different sectors; a fund tracking the **BSE Sensex** gives access to as many as **30 stocks** in one fund.
Deduction up to **₹1.5 lakh** by investing in **ELSS** under **Section 80C** of the Income Tax Act; ELSS has a **3-year lock-in**.

blocks.text: The source also describes an **indexation benefit** on debt funds, where only returns above the inflation rate (through the **Cost Inflation Index, CII**) were taxed, unlike ordinary interest which is fully taxable. Tax rules on debt funds have changed in recent years, so do not treat indexation as a current rule without checking the latest Income Tax provisions.

blocks.title: ELSS in one line: 3 - 1.5 - 80C
blocks.phrase: Three-year lock, one-and-a-half lakh limit, Section eighty-C.
letters: Years of lock-in; money can be withdrawn only afterwards
Income Tax Act section that gives the deduction
blocks.note: ELSS = Equity Linked Savings Scheme, an example of a tax saving fund.

blocks.title: Debt, equity and hybrid funds
rows: Relatively less risky; suit those wanting steady income and averse to risk
Higher risk because returns follow stock markets; capital appreciation is the aim; good for long-term goals like retirement or buying a house, as risk reduces over time
A mix of equity and fixed income
Sub-categories depend on the asset allocation between equity and debt

blocks.title: Debt, Equity, Hybrid
blocks.phrase: Debt = Dependable, Equity = Exciting (and risky), Hybrid = Half and half.
letters: Dependable: bonds and G-secs, lower risk
Exciting: stocks, higher risk and higher potential

blocks.title: Risks facing a debt fund
items: **Credit risk**: the issuer may default on interest or principal
**Interest rate volatility**: bond prices move opposite to rates, so falling rates help debt funds
Share price movements do **not** directly affect a pure debt fund

sections.title: Types by structure: open-ended and close-ended

blocks.title: Open-ended versus close-ended
rows: Redeem units on any business day at NAV
Bought and sold at the **Net Asset Value (NAV)**
Units are **listed** on the stock market like shares
Not very liquid because trading volumes are low

blocks.title: Open door, closed door
blocks.phrase: Open-ended = open door, walk in or out any business day at NAV. Close-ended = closed door till maturity; exit only by selling on the exchange.
letters: Any business day, at NAV, very liquid
Launch-time entry, maturity exit, listed, thinly traded

blocks.title: Capital Protection Oriented Schemes
blocks.text: **Capital Protection Oriented Schemes** are always **close-ended**, since the capital protection depends on the fund running to its fixed maturity.

blocks.title: Objective-based funds
rows: Aim for **capital appreciation**; put a big share into stocks; riskier, best held for the **long term**, and better avoided when you are close to your goal.
Aim for a **stable income**; debt funds investing mostly in bonds, government securities and certificates of deposit; suit lower-risk appetite.
Invest in **short-term money market instruments** such as treasury bills, CDs, term deposits and commercial papers; used to **park surplus money** for days to months or build an emergency fund.
Give tax benefits under **Section 80C** (deduction up to ₹1.5 lakh a year); **ELSS** is the example.

blocks.title: Objective funds: GILT
blocks.phrase: Pick GILT-edged goals: Growth, Income, Liquid, Tax-saving.
letters: Growth funds: capital appreciation, long term
Liquid funds: short-term money market parking
blocks.note: GILT here is only a memory trick; a separate type called Gilt funds invests in government securities.

blocks.title: Matching investor and fund
blocks.text: A young investor needing growth should hold more **equity growth funds**; someone wanting safety of principal, such as in a **money market fund**, picks liquid or debt options.

sections.title: NAV, SIP, SWP and other terms

blocks.title: Key terms
rows: Value of one unit of the fund: (total assets minus liabilities) divided by the number of units outstanding. Open-ended funds are bought and sold at NAV.
The share of a mutual fund scheme an investor holds; subscriptions are accounted for as **unit capital**.
Invest a fixed amount at regular intervals; a standard example of **rupee cost averaging**.
Lets an investor withdraw from a scheme at regular intervals, for example every month on set dates.
Moves money from one scheme to another at regular intervals.
Equity Linked Savings Scheme: tax saving, 3-year lock-in.
The document that lays down the **rights of investors** in a scheme.

blocks.title: NAV formula: A minus L over U
blocks.phrase: NAV = (Assets minus Liabilities) divided by Units.
letters: Assets: market value of the fund’s holdings plus cash
Liabilities: expenses and dues of the fund

blocks.title: SIP in, SWP out, STP across
blocks.phrase: SIP sips money in, SWP sips money out, STP switches it across.
letters: Systematic Transfer Plan: transfers between schemes

blocks.title: Facts from the exam point of view
rows: As per a SEBI norm (2018), investors may buy mutual funds worth up to **₹50,000** through digital wallets.
Mutual fund agents and distributors are paid **commissions**.
Debt mutual funds must keep a minimum of **10%** of assets in liquid holdings such as G-secs, cash, treasury bills and repo.
At the time of the source, domestic mutual funds could invest up to **USD 7 billion** in overseas stocks and an extra **USD 1 billion** in ETFs. Such limits change.
Cheque or demand draft, remittance, and ASBA (for new offers).

blocks.title: Not a benefit
blocks.text: Mutual fund investors do **not** hold physical custody of the securities in which the fund invests. Diversification, professional management and cost savings **are** benefits.

revision: A mutual fund **pools money** of many investors, managed by a fund manager of an **AMC**.
Mutual funds are regulated by **SEBI**; returns are market-linked and **not assured**.
Gains and losses are shared **in proportion to contribution**.
Four benefits: professional expertise, returns, diversification, tax benefits.
A fund tracking the **BSE Sensex** gives access to as many as **30 stocks**.
**ELSS**: deduction up to **₹1.5 lakh** under **Section 80C**; **3-year lock-in**.
**Open-ended** funds: buy or redeem any business day at **NAV**; **close-ended** funds have a maturity and are listed.
**Liquid funds** invest in treasury bills, CDs, commercial papers; park surplus money for days to months.
**NAV** = (assets minus liabilities) divided by units outstanding.
**SIP** is rupee cost averaging; **SWP** is regular withdrawal; **STP** transfers between schemes.
Debt funds must hold a minimum of **10%** in liquid holdings; **Capital Protection Oriented Schemes** are close-ended.
SEBI norm of 2018: purchases up to **₹50,000** through digital wallets.
